name: Lattice Reduction for Subset Sum (LLL, BKZ, Lagarias-Odlyzko)
description: Lattice reduction attacks embed a subset-sum instance into an integer lattice so that the planted 0/1 solution corresponds to an unusually short (or close) lattice vector; running LLL or BKZ then recovers the solution. Lagarias and Odlyzko (JACM 1985) built the canonical lattice and showed that with an exact shortest-vector oracle almost all instances of density d < 0.6463 are solved in polynomial time; Coster, Joux, LaMacchia, Odlyzko, Schnorr and Stern (1991/1992) modified the lattice and raised the density threshold to d < 0.9408. In practice one replaces the SVP oracle by LLL (polynomial time, weak approximation) or BKZ with block size beta (exponentially better quality at exponential cost). These methods are average-case/heuristic: they succeed on almost all random low-density knapsacks, degrade near density 1 (the hardest regime), and give no worst-case algorithm for general Subset Sum. They are a main source of conditional hardness for knapsack cryptosystems and are directly cryptanalytic rather than an exponential-time worst-case technique.
worst_case_time: As an exact worst-case Subset Sum algorithm there is no proven bound: general Subset Sum is NP-hard and the lattice reduction step (SVP) is NP-hard. LLL itself is polynomial time, O(n^5 B^3) bit operations for an n-dimensional basis with B-bit entries (space O(n^2) integers), but it only gives a 2^{O(n)}-approximate shortest vector. BKZ with block size beta costs roughly 2^{O(beta log beta)} per tour with an enumeration SVP oracle, or 2^{Theta(beta)} (about 2^{0.292 beta} with sieving) per SVP call, plus poly(n) per tour; this is super-polynomial in beta. Conditional guarantee: if a perfect SVP/CVP oracle is available, almost all random instances with density d < 0.9408 are solved in polynomial time. No O*(2^{c n}) worst-case bound for general Subset Sum follows.
space_complexity: LLL: polynomial, O(n^2) lattice memory (O(n^2 log B) bits). BKZ: polynomial O(n^2) memory for the basis plus the enumeration tree; enumeration variants are polynomial-space. Sieving-based BKZ (e.g. G6K) trades time for memory and uses about 2^{Theta(beta)} space. No exponential space is inherent to LLL/BKZ enumeration.
model: Classical RAM / real-number (exact integer or rational) arithmetic on lattice bases; bit-complexity measured in bit operations. Sieving variants use large random-access memory. Classical only; quantum lattice reduction (e.g. quantum sieving) can speed the SVP subroutine but is not the classical attack considered here.
randomized_or_deterministic: LLL is deterministic. BKZ exists in deterministic and randomized forms; practical/high-quality BKZ (Schnorr-Euchner, BKZ 2.0, progressive BKZ) is randomized (random sampling, extreme pruning, rerandomization). The subset-sum attack itself is heuristic: it is expected to succeed with high probability on random low-density instances, and there is no proven worst-case success guarantee.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: Parameterized by the BKZ block size beta: larger beta gives a better approximation factor (roughly beta^{n/(2 beta)} root-Hermite factor) at exponentially higher time, and for sieving-based SVP also higher memory. Standard enumeration BKZ is polynomial-space with 2^{O(beta log beta)} time; sieving BKZ is 2^{Theta(beta)} time and 2^{Theta(beta)} space. This is a quality/cost tradeoff for the lattice primitive, not a subset-sum time-space tradeoff curve.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: No 2^{c n} record; the relevant records are density thresholds and quality factors. LLL (Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovasz, 1982) gives approximation factor about (4/3)^{n/2} (with Hermite constant), polynomial time. Lagarias-Odlyzko (1985): density d < 0.6463 with an SVP oracle. Coster et al. (1991/1992): density d < 0.9408. Schnorr-Euchner BKZ (1994) with block size 20 solves almost all subset-sum instances of dimension up to 58 at density close to 1; Schnorr-Shevchenko (2012) solve dimension-80 density-1 random knapsacks in under a minute on average (about 9.4x faster and much less space than the BCJ birthday attack). BKZ 2.0 (Chen-Nguyen, 2011) gives better security estimates.
problem_variant: Random low-density / hard-knapsack Subset Sum (cryptanalytic regime), including the Merkle-Hellman and related knapsack cryptosystems. The hardest knapsacks have density slightly above 1 (about 1 + log2(n/2)/n). Not Equal-Subset-Sum / Pigeonhole ESS, not Partition, and not the general worst-case decision problem.
applies_to: Subset Sum with {0,1} coefficients on large integers (sparse/low-density instances), for which almost all instances of density below the threshold are solved given a sufficiently strong SVP/CVP oracle. Practical LLL/BKZ performs well for low density and dimensions up to a few hundred; it fails or becomes infeasible near density 1 and in high dimension. Extended variants with coefficients {-1,0,1} are covered by related analyses (Li-Ma, d < 0.488).
coefficient_set: C = {0,1} for the standard attack (solution vector e in {0,1}^n, mapped to a short vector with entries e_i - 1/2 up to scaling). Extended low-density analyses use ternary coefficients C = {-1,0,1} (e.g. Li-Ma, with density threshold 0.488).
density_regime: Low density d = n / log2(max_i a_i). SOLVED regimes under an SVP oracle: d < 0.6463 (Lagarias-Odlyzko 1985) and d < 0.9408 (Coster et al. 1991/1992). HARD regime: density close to 1 (empirically hardest around d ~ 1 + log2(n/2)/n), where the planted vector is no longer uniquely shortest and LLL/BKZ fail. High density (d > n/(n - log2 n), i.e. small numbers) is easier via DP/pseudopolynomial methods and cannot be injective for encryption. This is explicitly an average-case/density dichotomy, not a worst-case guarantee.
solution_regime: Average-case / almost-all low-density instances, treated as promised or unique-solution (for sparse knapsacks the solution is unique with high probability). Not a pigeonhole/many-solution regime and not a general decision procedure for arbitrary instances.
cardinality_constraint: No. The basic lattice attacks do not impose a fixed-cardinality (Hamming-weight) constraint; the solution weight is determined by the instance. Low-weight knapsack variants (e.g. Stern) are a separate line.
key_technique: Construct a lattice whose short vectors encode subsets (the Lagarias-Odlyzko lattice; Coster et al.'s CJLOSS modification, often with an extra coordinate to turn the inhomogeneous equation into a homogeneous short-vector problem) and run lattice basis reduction (LLL/BKZ, or an exact SVP/CVP oracle) to find the target short vector. BKZ generalizes LLL: for block size beta it repeatedly finds a shortest vector in each projected beta-dimensional block using an SVP subroutine (enumeration or sieving) and LLL-reduces, trading exponential time for a better approximation factor and hence a higher solvable density.
core_idea: The a_i and target T define an affine lattice in which the characteristic subset vector e corresponds to a lattice vector that is much shorter than generic vectors when the density is low; if this vector is the unique shortest one, an exact SVP solver returns it and the subset is read off. LLL finds only an approximate shortest vector but is cheap and suffices well below the threshold; larger BKZ blocks approximate SVP better, extending the density range at exponential cost. Above the density threshold the planted vector's length is comparable to that of other lattice vectors, so no reduction algorithm can reliably isolate it - this is exactly why density-1 knapsacks are cryptographically 'hard'.
reduction_pipeline: Subset Sum -> shortest/closest vector problem in a constructed integer lattice (Lagarias-Odlyzko lattice / Coster et al. modification; also modular variants with an extra congruence coordinate). Direction: Subset Sum reduces to lattice SVP/CVP; solve SVP by LLL/BKZ/enumeration/sieving. Related to simultaneous Diophantine approximation and to Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham small-root methods.
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: when lattice reduction (or an SVP oracle) returns the planted short vector, the attack outputs an explicit 0/1 witness. The guarantee is conditional on the reduction being strong enough and the instance being low-density/random; there is no existential-only variant.
search_vs_decision_witness: Search/witness: the successful attack returns the subset e in {0,1}^n. There is no worst-case decision guarantee; for hard instances the method simply fails to find a solution.
obstacle_to_2n3: Lattice reduction gives a polynomial-time average-case solution for low-density instances and a super-polynomial (but cryptanalytically practical) approach near the edge; it does not yield any worst-case exponential speedup. Near density 1 the planted vector is not uniquely shortest, so there is nothing for the reduction to find, and the general problem remains NP-hard. Consequently this line provides no O*(2^{(1/2-eps)n}) worst-case algorithm, let alone 2^{n/3}; it is orthogonal to the worst-case MITM barrier and mostly serves to explain why certain knapsacks are easy (low density) and why hard knapsacks (density ~1) resist lattice attacks.
potential_to_break_mitm: Low. It is an average-case/polynomial-time cryptanalytic technique for a restricted density regime; it neither targets the worst-case general problem nor improves the 2^{n/2} worst-case baseline, so it is unlikely to break the worst-case MITM barrier.
barrier_evidence: The density thresholds (0.6463 for Lagarias-Odlyzko, 0.9408 for Coster et al.) are asymptotic average-case guarantees that have resisted worst-case transfer; SVP is NP-hard and no polynomial algorithm solves it exactly. Above density ~0.94 the target vector is not uniquely shortest, and no known lattice algorithm recovers it in high dimension. Lattice methods inherently need random-like instances. Independent conditional lower bounds (SETH-based, Abboud-Bringmann-Hermelin-Shabtay) show Subset Sum cannot be solved in near-linear/near-quadratic time, and average-case k-SUM/hard-knapsack conjectures define hardness at density 1.
open_questions: Can the low-density threshold be pushed closer to 1 (and past it)? Is there a rigorous theory of BKZ on density-1 instances and its scaling in n and beta? What is the exact practical crossover between BKZ and generalized-birthday/representation attacks at density 1? Can lattice attacks be turned into worst-case algorithms or connected to the worst-case MITM barrier? Can sieving-based BKZ solve density-1 instances at cryptographically relevant dimension, and how do quantum sieving algorithms change this?
conditional_hypothesis: Correctness rests on the heuristic/average-case assumption that for random low-density instances the planted solution maps to the unique (or sufficiently separated) shortest lattice vector. Hardness statements rest on NP-hardness of subset sum and SVP, on concrete lattice-hardness (Hermite-factor) assumptions used to estimate BKZ cost, and on SETH-based lower bounds (Abboud et al.) for polynomial-time solvability. This is not a single universally named conjecture; the relevant 'low-density subset sum' and 'unique-SVP' assumptions are heuristic.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Average-case only, and heuristic. The density-threshold theorems say 'almost all' random instances of density below the threshold are solved (given a sufficiently strong SVP oracle). There is no worst-case guarantee: adversarial dense/structured instances and density-~1 instances are not covered.
cryptographic_regime: Directly cryptanalytic. The Lagarias-Odlyzko / Coster et al. attacks broke Merkle-Hellman and many knapsack public-key cryptosystems, and low-density knapsack instances with n public weights can be solved in polynomial time when d < 0.9408 (with an SVP oracle). Hard knapsacks at density ~1 are the target regime where representation/birthday attacks (HGJ/BCJ/BBSS) take over; lattice reduction is the reason those cryptosystems are insecure at low density and the reason density-1 parameter choices are used.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Complementary regime split. Dynamic-programming/pseudopolynomial algorithms solve dense instances (small integers, high/medium density); lattice reduction solves sparse low-density instances (large integers). The two families meet around density ~1, which is empirically the hardest regime. Lattice reduction does not combine with DP in a single algorithm; it is the 'large-number' counterpart to the 'small-number' DP approach.

empirical_evidence: Substantial empirical work. Schnorr-Euchner (1994) report that block Korkin-Zolotarev reduction with block size 20 solves almost all subset-sum instances of dimension up to 58 even at density close to 1, and their strongest algorithm solves almost all instances with up to 66 random weights. Schnorr-Shevchenko (2012) report solving 50 random dimension-80 density-1 knapsacks in roughly 9.4x less time and much less space than the Becker-Coron-Joux birthday attack (under a minute on average vs. about 15 hours). Gama-Nguyen (2008) and Chen-Nguyen (2011) provide extensive experiments/simulations of LLL/BKZ quality and cost. [uncertain] for exact modern benchmark tables.
implementation_artifact: Mature open-source lattice libraries are available. fplll: https://github.com/fplll/fplll (LLL/BKZ, floating-point). G6K: https://github.com/fplll/g6k (sieving, high-block-size BKZ). NTL: https://libntl.org/ (LLL, BKZ, Schnorr-Euchner). The lattice estimator for concrete cost/security estimates: https://github.com/malb/lattice-estimator. No single canonical repository implements the full knapsack attack end-to-end, but building one from these primitives is standard. [uncertain] regarding an official author implementation of the original attacks.
verification_method: Reproduce the lattice construction (Lagarias-Odlyzko / Coster et al.) and run an LLL/BKZ implementation (fplll, NTL, G6K) on random low-density knapsacks, sweeping the density d = n/log2(max a_i) and checking whether the planted subset is recovered; separately verify the density-threshold theorems by substituting an exact SVP solver (e.g. enumeration for small n) and observing that for d < 0.9408 the planted vector is the shortest. Checking the Merkle-Hellman break is a concrete end-to-end test. For cost claims, use the Chen-Nguyen/Gama-Nguyen simulation or the lattice estimator.
